voyager-1.tagline: The most distant machine humanity has built is still listening to the space between the stars.
voyager-1.dek: Launched in 1977 to visit Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to cross the heliopause and sample interstellar space directly.

paragraphs: In the late 1970s the four giant planets lined up in a way that happens only about once every 175 years, so a single spacecraft could swing from one to the next, borrowing speed from each planet’s gravity. NASA built two spacecraft to use that alignment. Voyager 2 left Earth on 20 August 1977. Voyager 1 followed on 5 September 1977 on a faster, shorter path to Jupiter and Saturn.

Voyager 1 rose from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on a Titan-Centaur rocket, with a launch mass of 723 kg. Its stated objectives were close-up studies of Jupiter, Saturn, their rings and larger moons, and then an exploration of the outermost edge of the Sun’s domain, the heliosphere. The planned mission was roughly five years long.

The route was a sequence of gravity assists. At Jupiter, Voyager 1 passed through a system that had only ever been seen from Earth as small discs. At Saturn, a close pass of the moon Titan bent its path north, out of the plane of the planets, which ended its planetary tour and sent it toward interstellar space.
Its last act as a camera platform came in 1990. Voyager 1 turned around, photographed the planets it had left behind, and then had its cameras switched off to save power.

timeline.title: Launch
timeline.text: Voyager 1 lifts off from Cape Canaveral on a Titan-Centaur.

timeline.title: Jupiter encounter
timeline.text: Closest approach to Jupiter. Three days later a look back at Io reveals an erupting volcano.

timeline.title: Io’s volcano found
timeline.text: JPL engineer Linda Morabito spots a curved cloud on the limb of Io in a Voyager 1 image.

timeline.title: Saturn and Titan
timeline.text: Voyager 1 flies past Titan and Saturn. The Titan pass deflects it out of the plane of the planets.

timeline.title: Family Portrait
timeline.text: From about 6 billion km, Voyager 1 takes a mosaic of the Solar System including the Pale Blue Dot frame. Its cameras are switched off afterwards.

timeline.title: Heliopause crossed
timeline.text: Particle data mark the date Voyager 1 passed into interstellar space. Plasma-wave measurements confirming it were announced in 2013.

timeline.title: Cosmic Ray Subsystem off
timeline.text: Switched off to save power.

timeline.title: LECP off
timeline.text: The Low-Energy Charged Particles experiment is switched off. Two science instruments remain on.

timeline.title: “Big Bang” power swap
timeline.text: Engineers replace three powered devices, including old tape-recorder hardware, with lower-power alternatives in one operation, to avoid shutting down another instrument as early as summer 2027.

timeline.title: Brief communications pause
timeline.text: Contact is lost for about 48 hours and then restored.

timeline.title: One light-day (projected)
timeline.text: NASA projects Voyager 1 will be 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion km) from Earth at 5:16 a.m. US Eastern time, where a one-way radio signal takes 24 hours.

paragraphs: Voyager 1 carried ten science instruments, or eleven investigations if radio science is counted separately. Most were designed for the planets. A few turned out to be exactly what was needed for the next frontier.

instruments.name: Imaging Science System (cameras)
instruments.role: Photographed Jupiter, Saturn and their moons, and the 1990 Family Portrait.

instruments.name: Infrared Interferometer Spectrometer and Radiometer (IRIS)
instruments.role: Measured temperatures and composition. At Io it found the hottest region, the lava lake at Loki.
instruments.status: Powered down; see NASA’s live status page

instruments.name: Plasma Science (PLS)
instruments.role: Measured the speed, density and temperature of charged particles in the solar wind.

instruments.name: Cosmic Ray Subsystem (CRS)
instruments.role: Counted high-energy particles arriving from the galaxy.

instruments.name: Low-Energy Charged Particles (LECP)
instruments.role: Tracked lower-energy ions and electrons, including particles from the Sun.

instruments.name: Magnetometer (MAG)
instruments.role: Measures the strength and direction of magnetic fields.

instruments.name: Plasma Wave Subsystem (PWS)
instruments.role: Listens to waves in plasma, which reveal how dense it is.

paragraphs: Voyager 1 is a single machine, but it is made of parts with very different jobs and very different fates.

entities.name: Voyager 1 spacecraft bus
entities.location: Interstellar space, in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus
entities.text: A ten-sided electronics bus carries a 3.7-metre dish antenna that points at Earth, three radioisotope thermoelectric generators that turn the heat of decaying plutonium into electricity, and instruments on booms. The magnetometer sits on a boom roughly 13 metres long, away from the spacecraft’s own magnetic noise. The generators lose about 4 watts of power every year, which is why instruments are being switched off one by one.

entities.name: The Golden Record
entities.condition: Intact (as recorded in the mission data)
entities.text: A 12-inch gold-plated copper phonograph record with a cover that shows how to play it. It carries 115 images, natural sounds, about 90 minutes of music from many cultures and greetings in 55 languages. It was chosen by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan as a message for any future finder, not as a scientific instrument.

paragraphs: Voyager 1 does not have an afterlife yet. It is still transmitting, so this chapter is a status report, not an obituary. NASA lists no last-contact date and no end-of-mission date, and this archive does not invent one.

NASA has said that without the September 2026 power swap another science instrument would have had to be switched off as early as summer 2027. Eventually the generators will not be able to run the transmitter. At that point Voyager 1 will keep coasting silently. NASA has said that in about 40,000 years it will pass within about 1.7 light-years of the star Gliese 445.

status.label: Instrument status
status.value: 2 of 10 science instruments on: magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem (NASA, April 2026)

status.label: Last contact
status.value: None: contact is continuing. A brief pause on 20 Oct 2026 lasted about 48 hours.

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: Everything, in motion: the spacecraft and the Golden Record travel together out of the Solar System.

paragraphs: Voyager 1 changed what we think the outer Solar System is: not a set of quiet, cratered moons but worlds with volcanoes, thick atmospheres and rings. Then it changed what we think the edge of the Sun’s domain is, by crossing it.

It also changed how people see the Earth. The Pale Blue Dot photograph inspired the title of Carl Sagan’s 1994 book, and the Golden Record made a spacecraft into a message. As engineering, Voyager 1 is a lesson in what careful design, patient operations and nuclear power can do: commands now take 24 hours to arrive and a reply takes 24 more.

inherited.before: Before Voyager 1, Jupiter, Saturn and their moons were known only from Earth-based telescopes and a few earlier flybys. No one had seen volcanism erupting anywhere beyond Earth, and the boundary where the Sun’s wind gives way to interstellar space was a theoretical prediction that no instrument had ever reached.

instrument.name: Plasma Wave Subsystem (PWS)
instrument.how: The PWS uses two long electric antennas to listen to waves in the plasma around the spacecraft. A plasma rings at a natural frequency that depends on how many charged particles it holds: the denser it is, the higher the note. When the Sun throws out a large burst, it sends a shock through the plasma that makes it ring. By reading the pitch of that ring, scientists can work out the density without a particle counter ever touching the gas. The pitch turned out to be a few kilohertz.

evidence: At Io, a Voyager 1 camera frame taken on 8 March 1979 showed a bright curved cloud on the limb, and earlier frames from 4 March show a plume rising more than 100 km above the surface. IRIS found several regions hundreds of degrees Fahrenheit warmer than their surroundings, and Loki’s lava lake was about 150 °C warmer than its neighbourhood.

At the heliopause, the particle instruments recorded the solar-particle count falling and galactic cosmic rays rising around 25 August 2012. Later, the PWS heard the plasma ringing after solar outbursts in 2012 and 2013. The pitch of that ringing meant the plasma was about 40 times denser than the plasma just inside the boundary.
inherited.breakthrough: Io became the first body beyond Earth where active volcanism was observed, and Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to measure interstellar plasma directly.

directVsInterpreted.text: Plumes and hot spots on Io, seen in camera and infrared data.
Tidal heating, the squeezing of Io by Jupiter and by Europa’s gravity, is the likely heat source.
A jump in plasma density and in cosmic-ray counts at the heliopause.
Where the whole boundary is and how the heliosphere is shaped come from combining Voyager’s two paths with models.

inherited.legacy: Voyager’s Io discovery defined a research target that later missions, including the Galileo orbiter at Jupiter, studied for years. Its heliopause crossing gave models of the heliosphere real data, and Voyager 2’s later crossing in November 2018 provided a second line through the boundary.
inherited.technology: Voyager 1 also proved a technology: a 1970s spacecraft powered by a radioisotope generator can keep working, and be repaired by commands that take a day to reach it, for almost half a century.

before: Active volcanism known only on Earth
after: Io seen erupting, with hot lava lakes
Interstellar plasma measured directly
Titan shown to have a thick atmosphere

spotlight.headline: Io: the first volcano ever seen erupting beyond Earth
spotlight.text: Four days after Voyager 1’s closest approach to Jupiter, a JPL engineer examining a navigation frame noticed a strange crescent rising from the edge of Io. It was an eruption plume, rising high enough to catch sunlight against black sky. Within days the team had located more eruptions, and the infrared instrument had matched them to hot spots.
evidence: Plume more than 100 km high in the 4 March 1979 image
IRIS: hot regions several hundred °F above their surroundings
At least four eruptions identified on Voyager 1 pictures

science instruments still on in 2026: magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem
Earth’s distance when the Pale Blue Dot was photographed, 14 February 1990
electrical power lost every year as the plutonium decays

ripple.title: Voyager 2 at the heliopause
ripple.text: Voyager 2 crossed in November 2018 on a different path, so scientists could compare two measurements of the boundary.

ripple.title: Galileo at Jupiter
ripple.text: Io’s volcanoes became a long-term target for later Jupiter missions.

ripple.title: Titan
ripple.text: Voyager 1’s Titan flyby revealed a thick atmosphere, making Titan a reason for later missions to Saturn.

ripple.title: The Pale Blue Dot
ripple.text: The 1990 image gave a name to a way of seeing Earth, and inspired Carl Sagan’s book.

unanswered.question: What lies beyond the Sun’s influence, and what shape is the heliosphere?
unanswered.text: Voyager 1 is one thin line through a huge region, with only two instruments left to read it. Scientists still debate the shape of the heliosphere and how the interstellar magnetic field and plasma change farther out.
unanswered.future: Concept studies for a dedicated interstellar probe exist, but no such mission is currently flying. Until then, every month of Voyager data is irreplaceable.

alsep.tagline: Five silent stations still sit on the Moon, where for eight years they felt it shake.
alsep.dek: The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package turned five landing sites into the first permanent scientific stations on another world.

paragraphs: The first astronauts on the Moon carried a simple experiment package that worked only for a short time. Apollo 11’s early package held a seismometer and a laser reflector. The scientists who wanted to understand the Moon needed something that would keep running after the crew left, and that is what ALSEP was.

ALSEP stood for Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package. Each one was a set of instruments linked by cable to a central station that supplied power and radioed the data to Earth. Five stations were set up, by the crews of Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17. The goals in the mission data were to monitor the lunar environment continuously after the astronauts left, and to measure seismic activity, heat flow, the solar wind and the lunar atmosphere.

facts.label: Power
facts.value: SNAP-27 radioisotope generator at each station

paragraphs: ALSEP did not travel on its own. It rode to the Moon inside each lunar module, and astronauts carried it out on the surface, on foot or with the rover on later missions, and unpacked it. After they left, the stations kept sending data to Earth until the shutdown.

timeline.title: Apollo 12 launches
timeline.text: The first full ALSEP is on board.

timeline.title: First ALSEP deployed
timeline.text: Apollo 12 astronauts set up the first station in Oceanus Procellarum.

timeline.title: Apollo 14 and Apollo 15
timeline.text: Two more stations. Apollo 15 adds a heat-flow experiment.

timeline.title: Apollo 16 and Apollo 17
timeline.text: The last two stations. The seismic network now spans five sites.

timeline.title: Switched off
timeline.text: NASA commands all remaining stations off at the same time because of funding cuts.

paragraphs: No two stations carried exactly the same instruments, and many were run by different principal investigators. Together they made a seismic network, a magnetic survey, a particle monitor and a heat-flow probe.

instruments.name: Passive Seismic Experiment
instruments.role: A very sensitive seismometer that recorded moonquakes and meteoroid impacts at four sites (Apollo 12, 14, 15 and 16).

instruments.name: Heat Flow Experiment
instruments.role: Probes lowered into drill holes to measure how much heat flows out of the Moon (Apollo 15 and 17).

instruments.name: Lunar Surface Magnetometer
instruments.role: Measured the magnetic field at the surface and how it responds to the Sun.

instruments.name: Solar Wind Spectrometer
instruments.role: Measured the solar wind reaching the surface.

instruments.name: Cold Cathode Gauge and atmospheric experiments
instruments.role: Measured how much gas is above the surface. Apollo 17 added a mass spectrometer for the composition.

paragraphs: The mission data records ALSEP as one entry: multiple central stations and instruments left on the Moon at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 landing sites, all inactive. It helps to know what each part was.

entities.name: Central station
entities.location: Each of the five Apollo landing sites (12, 14, 15, 16, 17)
entities.text: A boxed electronics unit with a dish antenna that received commands and sent back the data. Astronauts aligned the antenna toward Earth by hand.

entities.name: SNAP-27 radioisotope generator
entities.condition: Inactive; the generators remain on the surface
entities.text: Heat from plutonium fuel produced electricity for years, and kept instruments warm through lunar nights that fall far below −150 °C.

entities.name: Experiments and cables
entities.location: Within a few tens of metres of each station
entities.text: Seismometers, magnetometers, heat probes and detectors, connected to the station by cable.

entities.name: Not ALSEP: the laser retroreflectors
entities.text: Corner-cube mirror arrays that reflect laser pulses from Earth. They are not part of ALSEP and need no power.

paragraphs: ALSEP did not fail. It was switched off. On 30 September 1977, because of budget cuts, NASA commanded all the remaining active stations off at the same time. That date is both the last contact and the end date in the mission record.

status.label: Spacecraft status
status.value: Inactive: every station has been off since 30 September 1977

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: Five central stations, their generators and instruments, at the Apollo 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17 sites

paragraphs: ALSEP was the first permanent scientific monitoring network on another world. Its seismic data are still being re-analysed with methods the Apollo scientists did not have, and the questions they raised about the Moon’s interior are still alive.

It also showed what long-term stations can do. Placing a seismometer on Mars decades later, as InSight did, followed the same idea: a single station on a planet reveals what is happening far beneath its surface.

inherited.before: Before ALSEP, scientists knew the Moon’s size and mass but could only guess what lay inside it. Was it molten, cold and solid all the way through, or layered like the Earth? Nobody had put a seismometer on another world and listened.

instrument.name: Passive Seismic Experiment
instrument.how: The seismometer works like a weight hanging from a spring. When the ground moves, the frame moves with it but the weight lags behind, and that difference is the signal. The instrument could detect ground motion of the order of a nanometre. It also needed protection: lunar nights are far colder than −150 °C, so the electronics were kept warm by heat from the station’s generator.

evidence: The network recorded several kinds of event: deep moonquakes far below the surface that recur with the lunar tides, shallow moonquakes, thermal quakes as the surface warms and cools, and meteoroid impacts.

Scientists also made their own signals. Spent rocket stages and lunar-module ascent stages were deliberately crashed onto the Moon, and the seismometers recorded signals that lasted far longer than similar impacts do on Earth.
The Apollo 15 and 17 heat probes measured heat flowing out of the Moon’s interior, and the atmospheric instruments measured a very thin gas that is closer to an exosphere than a true atmosphere.
inherited.breakthrough: The Moon’s interior is layered, with a crust, a mantle and a core, much as the Earth is. The Moon is also far quieter than the Earth: moonquakes are numerous but small.

directVsInterpreted.text: Seismic waves from quakes and impacts, recorded at several stations at once.
Heat flow measured at two sites, and a very thin gas near the surface.
Layer boundaries and thicknesses of crust, mantle and core, inferred by timing waves between stations.
How the Moon formed and cooled, which depends on how those layers are read.

inherited.legacy: ALSEP data are still being used. Later gravity maps and modern analysis methods refine the layer models, and a 2019 re-study linked some shallow moonquakes to young faults near the Apollo 17 site.
inherited.technology: ALSEP also demonstrated engineering that later missions depended on: long-lived radioisotope power, remote command of instruments on another world and instruments built to survive extreme temperature swings.

before: Whether the Moon was seismically active unknown
Surface gas thought absent or uncertain
after: Layered interior with a crust, mantle and core
Moonquakes recorded in several types
A thin exosphere measured

spotlight.headline: When humans crashed spacecraft on the Moon, it rang
spotlight.text: Scientists made use of the equipment astronauts were leaving behind. After they went home, spent lunar-module stages were steered into the surface on purpose. The impacts were known, so the seismometers could use them as test signals. The reverberations lasted far longer than they do on Earth, which told the team something about the dry, fractured upper layers of the Moon.
evidence: Impacts at known times and places used as calibration
Signals lasting much longer than comparable impacts on Earth

ripple.title: Seismology on Mars
ripple.text: InSight’s single seismic station on Mars, decades later, used the same approach: read a planet’s interior from the waves it makes.

ripple.title: Modern re-analysis
ripple.text: Apollo seismic records are still re-examined with modern methods, including a 2019 study that linked some shallow moonquakes to young faults.

ripple.title: Gravity and seismic data together
ripple.text: Later lunar gravity maps were combined with Apollo seismic data to refine models of crustal thickness.

unanswered.question: What is the Moon’s core really like?
unanswered.text: Every ALSEP seismometer sat on the near side of the Moon. The far side and the deep interior were poorly sampled, so the size and state of the core are still debated.
unanswered.future: New seismometers on the far side have been proposed, which would give the first view from the opposite hemisphere.

surveyor-3.tagline: The only robot on another world that humans ever walked up to and took apart.
surveyor-3.dek: Surveyor 3 proved the Moon’s surface could hold a lander, and two years later Apollo 12 astronauts walked over and brought parts of it home.

paragraphs: Before anyone could land a crew on the Moon, NASA needed to know what the surface was like. Some feared a deep layer of fine dust that could swallow a lander. The Surveyor programme sent robotic landers to find out, and Surveyor 3 was one of them.

It was launched on 17 April 1967 and landed in Oceanus Procellarum, the Ocean of Storms. It had three objectives in the mission data: make a soft landing to prove the technology for Apollo, take television pictures of the surface, and test lunar soil mechanics with a sampling scoop. Its landed mass was 296 kg.

facts.label: Landed
facts.value: Oceanus Procellarum, 19–20 April 1967 (date depends on time zone)

paragraphs: Surveyor 3 landed on the inside slope of a small crater. It dug trenches with its scoop, photographed them and the surrounding terrain, and sent data until the first lunar night closed in. Contact was lost on 4 May 1967. Then the story paused for two and a half years.

timeline.title: Soft landing

timeline.title: Trenching and imaging

paragraphs: Surveyor 3 carried two main tools for learning about the surface, and the whole point was soil. It did not carry a chemical analyser; later Surveyors did.

instruments.name: Television camera
instruments.role: Photographed the landing site, the sky, its own footpads and every trench the scoop dug.
instruments.status: Removed by Apollo 12 in 1969 and returned to Earth

instruments.name: Soil mechanics surface sampler
instruments.role: A scoop on an extendable arm that dug trenches, pressed on the soil and showed how it behaves.
instruments.status: Removed by Apollo 12 in 1969 and returned to Earth

paragraphs: Surveyor 3 is the rare spacecraft whose parts were split between two worlds.

entities.name: Surveyor 3 lander chassis
entities.condition: Inactive; the camera and scoop were removed by Apollo 12
entities.text: The frame, legs and electronics remain on the crater slope where the spacecraft landed.

entities.name: Television camera
entities.text: Conrad removed it so it could be studied after about two and a half years on the Moon.

entities.name: Soil scoop and other pieces
entities.text: The scoop and several other parts were brought back to see how materials behave after long exposure on the lunar surface.

paragraphs: Surveyor 3 was a success that ended without a ceremony: its signal simply stopped. Its second life began in 1969 when astronauts chose to land close to it as a test of precision.

status.label: Spacecraft status
status.value: Inactive since contact was lost on 4 May 1967

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: The chassis and legs on the Moon. The camera and scoop are on Earth.

paragraphs: Surveyor 3 helped give NASA confidence that a lunar module could land safely, and remains the only robotic probe visited by humans on another world. The Apollo 12 landing near it also showed that a crewed spacecraft could land within a few hundred metres of a chosen target.
The returned parts gave scientists a chance to examine hardware that had been exposed to the lunar surface for about 31 months, a study that is hard to arrange any other way.

inherited.before: Before the Surveyors, there was a real argument about whether the Moon was covered in deep, loose dust. If it was, a heavy lander might sink. Earlier landers had suggested the surface was firm, but engineers wanted measurements of how strong the soil was in different places.

instrument.name: Soil mechanics surface sampler
instrument.how: The sampler was a small scoop on a folding arm, controlled from Earth. Operators could push the scoop into the soil, drag it, press on it and dump what it held, while the camera watched. Because the force needed was known, the pictures turned into measurements: how deep it went, how steeply the trench walls stayed up and whether the soil crumbled.

evidence: The scoop dug trenches up to 17.5 cm deep. Photos of the trenches showed walls that held their shape.
The soil behaved as a granular material with some cohesion, firm enough to support the weight of the lander and, by extension, a larger crewed lander.
inherited.breakthrough: The lunar surface was strong enough to support a crewed landing, answering one of the biggest engineering worries of the Apollo programme.

directVsInterpreted.text: Trench depths and walls, and how the scoop moved through the soil.
That the soil would bear a crewed lander, which is an engineering conclusion drawn from those measurements.

inherited.legacy: The same idea, a scoop on an arm watched by a camera, became a standard way to study soil on other worlds.
inherited.technology: Surveyor 3 also supported landing technology and gave Apollo a ground-truth test: Apollo 12 landed about 180 m away.

before: No hardware had been studied after lunar exposure
after: Granular but cohesive soil that holds trenches
Surface judged firm enough for Apollo
Parts studied after about 31 months on the Moon

spotlight.headline: A robot that humans visited
spotlight.text: On 20 November 1969 Apollo 12 commander Pete Conrad walked into a small crater, stood beside Surveyor 3 and cut off its television camera. No other robotic probe on another world has been visited by humans. The camera went home with the crew.

unanswered.question: How does lunar dust behave over years of exposure?
unanswered.text: Surveyor 3 and its camera were coated in dust, some of it thrown up by the nearby Apollo landing. How lunar dust sticks to equipment and degrades it is still an engineering problem for future crews.
unanswered.future: Artemis-era missions are being designed with that lesson in mind.

sojourner.tagline: A seven-day experiment on wheels that ran for 83 days and changed how we explore other planets.
sojourner.dek: Sojourner was the first rover to drive on Mars. It tested rocks, soil and the idea that a robot could roam.

paragraphs: In the 1990s NASA wanted to show that Mars could be reached quickly and cheaply. Mars Pathfinder was the second mission in the low-cost Discovery programme. It had to land safely with a cocoon of airbags, with no orbit around Mars first, and then release a small rover that could drive around the lander.

Sojourner weighed 10.5 kg once deployed. It was launched on 4 December 1996. Its goals were to demonstrate cheap delivery to the surface and mobility on Mars, and to characterise the rocks and soil at the landing site in Ares Vallis, an ancient flood channel.

Sojourner never travelled far, but every metre was a first. The rover rolled down the lander’s rear ramp on 5 July 1997, the day after landing, and then worked its way from rock to rock, always staying within reach of the lander that relayed its signals.

paragraphs: Sojourner was both an experiment and an instrument carrier. Everything it did relied on the lander, which acted as radio relay and as the camera that photographed the rover at work.

entities.name: Sojourner rover
entities.text: A six-wheeled rover with a solar panel on top and the X-ray spectrometer mounted at the rear, controlled from Earth with a delay of minutes.

entities.name: Pathfinder lander (Carl Sagan Memorial Station)
entities.text: The lander was renamed in honour of Carl Sagan. Its deflated airbags and ramps remain around it.

paragraphs: Sojourner’s story has three different dates. The last data transmission from the lander arrived on 27 September 1997. NASA tried for five months to restore full communications. The mission was officially terminated on 10 March 1998. The mission data says Sojourner likely kept working on its own until its batteries ran out; there is no confirmation of that.

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: The rover and the lander in Ares Vallis

paragraphs: Sojourner showed that mobile science on another planet worked. Its successors, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance, followed the same recipe on a larger scale. The Mars Exploration Rovers also reused the airbag landing method.
Pathfinder’s results mattered too: rounded pebbles and cobbles pointed to ancient floods, and the rock chemistry showed how varied the crust is.

inherited.before: Before Pathfinder, Mars rocks had been studied only from orbit, from meteorites, and by landers that could examine only what lay within reach of their arms. Nobody had a mobile instrument on the surface to choose and test many rocks.

instrument.name: Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS)
instrument.how: The APXS holds a small radioactive source that fires alpha particles at the target. Atoms in the rock respond by sending out X-rays and other particles whose energies identify the elements. Sojourner could press the instrument against a rock or soil patch, so the reading was taken of the exact target scientists picked. That also made the result sensitive to dust or coatings on the rock’s surface.

evidence: The rock Barnacle Bill had a composition the team called andesitic, which could mean a true volcanic andesite or a physical mixture of particles.
The rock Yogi had a lower quartz content and looked more primitive, more like common basalts on Earth.
Pebbles and cobbles in the surrounding terrain were rounded, which points to transport by flowing water.
When Sojourner’s wheels dug in during a turn, they exposed bright white material below the surface.
inherited.breakthrough: Mars’s rocks were not all the same. The crust appeared more varied than expected, and the surroundings of Ares Vallis showed signs of flood deposits.

directVsInterpreted.text: Element measurements of named rocks and soils, and the shapes of pebbles and cobbles.
That the pebbles were shaped by flowing water, and what the silica contents say about Mars’s crust.
Whether Barnacle Bill is a true andesite or a mixture: the original caption left both possibilities open.

inherited.legacy: The APXS design flew again. Later Mars rovers carried improved versions, and landers have used the same pattern of “roll up and touch the rock” ever since.
inherited.technology: Sojourner also proved technology: driving autonomously with hazard detection under a long time delay, and a very low-cost approach to delivering a payload to Mars.

before: Mars rocks known only from orbit and meteorites
No mobile instrument on the surface
Flood channels interpreted only from orbit
after: In-situ chemistry of chosen rocks
Evidence for rounded, water-worn rocks at a flood site
A rover design that could be scaled up

spotlight.headline: Seven days planned, 83 delivered
spotlight.text: Pathfinder was designed for a short mission, with Sojourner planned for just a week of driving. Instead the pair kept working until the lander stopped transmitting in September 1997. The extra weeks let the team study a lot more rocks and soil, and learn how the rover handled dust and cold.
evidence: Planned seven-day mission for Sojourner
About 83 days of operations (NASA Photojournal)
Last data on 27 September 1997

numbers.label: deployed mass of Sojourner
planned lifetime, versus about 83 days of operations
final data transmission, 27 September 1997
date NASA ended the mission after five months of recovery attempts

ripple.title: Spirit and Opportunity
ripple.text: The Mars Exploration Rovers used airbag landings and carried an APXS of their own.

ripple.title: Curiosity and Perseverance
ripple.text: Both inherited Sojourner’s approach to hazard avoidance and instrument placement.

ripple.title: Low-cost Mars missions
ripple.text: Pathfinder showed that a small, focused mission could deliver big results.

unanswered.question: How long, and how wet, was early Mars?
unanswered.text: Sojourner saw rounded stones at a flood channel, but a single site cannot say how long water flowed or whether Mars was ever warm and wet for long.
unanswered.future: Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance each added more sites. Samples collected by Perseverance could someday be examined in laboratories on Earth.

notes: Confirmed: image captions (Barnacle Bill andesitic or mixture; Yogi low in quartz; wheels exposing white material; sol 22; last transmission 10:23 UTC 27 Sep 1997; terminated 10 Mar 1998; 83 days vs 7); mission data for launch, mass, coordinates.

From general knowledge, please verify: landing date 4 July 1997; airbag landing without orbit; MER airbag reuse; APXS descendants on later rovers; Discovery programme as second mission; that the lander was renamed for Sagan (in the mission data).

opportunity.tagline: Built for 90 days, it explored Mars for more than 14 years and found the planet had been soaked in water.
opportunity.dek: Opportunity drove 28.06 miles across Meridiani Planum and the rim of Endeavour Crater, reading Mars’s water history in rocks and tiny spherules.

paragraphs: Opportunity was the second of two twin Mars Exploration Rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, launched in the summer of 2003. NASA wanted rovers that could read the planet’s past: not just look at rocks but test them for signs of water. Opportunity (MER-B) was sent to Meridiani Planum, a flat plain where orbiting instruments had detected the mineral hematite, which on Earth often forms in the presence of water.

The rover weighed 185 kg and launched on 7 July 2003. Its mission, as recorded in the mission data, was to find out the aqueous, climatic and geologic history of a site where conditions may have favoured the preservation of evidence of possible past life, and to examine rocks and soils for clues to past water. Its primary mission was three months long.

Opportunity landed inside a small crater called Eagle and found its first big result almost at once. From there it drove from crater to crater, spent most of 2004 in Endurance Crater, then made a long trek of more than five kilometres south to Victoria Crater. Finally it reached the rim of Endeavour Crater, where it studied older rocks than anywhere else it had been.

timeline.title: Launch
timeline.text: Opportunity (MER-B) leaves Earth.

timeline.title: Landing in Eagle Crater
timeline.text: The rover lands on Meridiani Planum.

timeline.title: “Last Chance”
timeline.text: A rock studied close up shows embedded spherules that the team nicknames blueberries.

timeline.title: Prime mission complete
timeline.text: Opportunity finishes its three-month prime mission and keeps going.

timeline.title: Near Victoria Crater
timeline.text: After a trek of more than 5 km, the rover finds large spherules again on the ring of material around Victoria.

timeline.title: Kirkwood outcrop
timeline.text: At Endeavour Crater’s rim the rover finds spherules that look similar to the blueberries but are different.

timeline.title: Last communication
timeline.text: A planet-wide dust storm blocks sunlight from the rover’s solar panels.

timeline.title: Mission declared complete
timeline.text: After more than a thousand recovery commands, NASA ends the mission.

paragraphs: Opportunity was a mobile geology laboratory. Its cameras selected targets, its arm brought instruments to them, and a grinding tool cleaned off dust and weathered surfaces first.

instruments.name: Panoramic Camera (Pancam) and Navigation Camera
instruments.role: Colour and navigation imaging of the terrain.

instruments.name: Miniature Thermal Emission Spectrometer (Mini-TES)
instruments.role: Identified minerals from their infrared glow.

instruments.name: Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer (APXS)
instruments.role: Measured the elements in rocks and soil.

instruments.name: Mössbauer Spectrometer
instruments.role: Identified iron-bearing minerals and their states.

instruments.name: Microscopic Imager
instruments.role: Took close-up images of rocks and soil a few centimetres across.

instruments.name: Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT)
instruments.role: Ground away dust and weathered surface to expose fresh rock.

paragraphs: Opportunity itself is one object, left where it stopped. Around Mars lies other hardware from its journey.

entities.name: Opportunity rover
entities.location: Perseverance Valley, Endeavour Crater (2.28° S, 354.47° E)
entities.text: A six-wheeled solar-powered rover that carried cameras, spectrometers and a rock-grinding arm. Dust on its solar panels, then a global storm, ended its operations.

entities.name: Landing platform
entities.text: The lander platform that carried Opportunity to the surface remains at the landing site, where the rover first drove off.

paragraphs: Opportunity’s end has two dates: the last time it spoke and the day NASA gave up listening. The storm that began in mid-2018 covered the planet in dust, and the rover’s solar panels could not make enough power. Its last communication was on 10 June 2018. Engineers then sent more than a thousand recovery commands over the following months, and declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019.

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: The rover in Perseverance Valley and the landing platform in Eagle Crater

paragraphs: Opportunity was designed for 90 days and explored Mars for more than 14 years, driving an off-world record of 28.06 miles (about 45 km). Its observations rewrote the history of water on Mars, showing that ancient water in some places was salty and acidic, and in others, by the time it reached Endeavour, more benign.
It left a method behind: choose a site by the minerals, then test by touching. Later rovers use the same approach.

inherited.before: Before Opportunity, orbiting instruments had detected hematite across Meridiani Planum, which suggested water might have been involved. But that mineral can form in other ways, so scientists did not know whether water had really been there, what it was like, or whether it had been abundant or merely a passing film.

instrument.name: Rock Abrasion Tool
instrument.how: Mars is covered in dust and its rocks are weathered, so the outside of a rock does not reveal what it is made of. The Rock Abrasion Tool ground into a rock with a spinning wheel, then brushed the powder away so the other instruments could read fresh material. One hole, on a rock called Pilbara, was 4.5 cm wide and just 7.2 mm deep, and cut straight through one of the spherules so its inside could be seen.

evidence: The rocks at the landing site held small round spherules that reminded researchers of berries in a muffin. They were analysed as hematite-rich concretions: mineral grains that grow inside rock soaked with water.
A spectrometer that identifies iron minerals found evidence of minerals that form in acidic water, so the groundwater at this site was acidic.

At Endeavour Crater, Opportunity found veins of gypsum, a mineral deposited by water flowing through underground fractures, plus spherules at Kirkwood that did not have the blueberries’ iron-rich composition.
inherited.breakthrough: Liquid water had once saturated the surface at Meridiani Planum for long enough to leave deposits behind. That turned an orbital hint into a measured fact.

directVsInterpreted.text: Spherules embedded in rock, their hematite-rich composition, and gypsum veins.
That groundwater formed the concretions, and that it was acidic and salty.
Whether such water could have supported life. Opportunity found evidence of water and chemistry, not evidence of life.

inherited.legacy: Opportunity’s “follow the water” results shaped where later rovers were sent and how they work. Perseverance also grinds rock surfaces clean before analysing them.
inherited.technology: Opportunity also proved a technology: a solar-powered rover can survive Martian winters, and recover from dust, for more than a decade.

before: Hematite seen from orbit, origin unclear
Unknown whether water had pooled at the site
after: Concretions formed in water-soaked rock
Acidic, salty groundwater identified
Rover lifetimes measured in years

spotlight.headline: Blueberries, and the spherules that are not blueberries
spotlight.text: The little spheres that Opportunity found in 2004 told scientists that water had soaked the rock. Eight years later, at Kirkwood outcrop, the rover found spheres that looked just like them. They were not made of the same iron-rich material, and some had concentric internal layers. Science did not repeat itself: it got a new puzzle.
evidence: Hematite-rich concretions identified in 2004
Kirkwood spherules up to about 3 mm wide, with a different composition
Concentric internal structure where some are eroded

numbers.label: planned prime mission, versus more than 14 years of operation
distance driven, an off-world record (about 45 km)
depth of the hole the Rock Abrasion Tool ground into the rock Pilbara
recovery commands sent after the 2018 dust storm
trek south from Endurance to Victoria Crater

ripple.title: Curiosity and Perseverance
ripple.text: Later rovers were sent to places where water-lain deposits were visible from orbit.

ripple.title: Abrasion as standard practice
ripple.text: Grinding away weathered surfaces before analysis is now routine on Mars.

ripple.title: Rovers as long-term observers
ripple.text: Opportunity showed that a single machine can watch a landscape through dust storms and seasons for years.

unanswered.question: Was ancient Meridiani water ever habitable?
unanswered.text: Opportunity found that water had been present, but the water at its landing site was acidic and salty, which is hard on life. Whether there were gentler places and times on Mars, and whether life ever existed, is still unknown. No mission has found evidence of life on Mars.
unanswered.future: Perseverance is collecting rock samples that could be examined in Earth laboratories if they are returned.

sources.label: NASA Photojournal PIA19113, blueberries near Fram

From general knowledge, please verify: landing in Eagle Crater in January 2004; Mössbauer detection of acid-water minerals (jarosite); instrument list and roles; Challenger Memorial Station name (not used in text); Curiosity/Perseverance sites; Perseverance abrasion.

insight.tagline: The first lander that listened to the inside of another planet.
insight.dek: InSight put a seismometer on the Martian ground and heard more than 1,300 marsquakes, enough to map the planet’s crust, mantle and liquid core.

paragraphs: Most of what we know about Mars is about its surface. InSight was built to look inside: it was named for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport, and it was designed to understand how rocky planets form and evolve by studying the structure and processes of Mars’s interior.

InSight was a joint effort: NASA and JPL led it, France’s space agency CNES provided the seismometer and Germany’s DLR provided a heat probe. It was launched on 5 May 2018 and landed in Elysium Planitia. Its landed mass was 358 kg. The mission was planned to last one Martian year, about two Earth years.
InSight did not move. Its journey after landing was the careful deployment of its instruments with a 2.4-metre robotic arm, then four years of listening.

timeline.title: Launch
timeline.text: InSight leaves for Mars.

timeline.title: Landing
timeline.text: The lander touches down in Elysium Planitia.

timeline.title: Survey of the deck
timeline.text: The deployment camera photographs its own deck and the two science instruments still on it.

timeline.title: SEIS placed on the ground
timeline.text: The first time a spacecraft robotically placed a seismometer onto another planet.

timeline.title: Wind and thermal shield added
timeline.text: The arm places a dome over the seismometer.

timeline.title: Listening
timeline.text: SEIS records marsquakes and impacts for years.

timeline.title: Last contact and end of mission
timeline.text: Dust on the solar panels has cut power. After two missed communication sessions NASA retires the mission.

paragraphs: Three main experiments covered Mars’s interior in different ways: waves, rotation and heat.

instruments.name: SEIS (Seismic Experiment for Interior Structure)
instruments.role: A seismometer provided by CNES that listened for marsquakes and meteorite impacts.

instruments.name: HP3 (Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package)
instruments.role: A heat probe from DLR meant to burrow beneath the surface and measure heat flowing from the interior.
instruments.status: Did not burrow to the planned depth; inactive

instruments.name: RISE (Rotation and Interior Structure Experiment)
instruments.role: Tracked the lander’s radio signal to measure tiny wobbles in Mars’s spin that depend on its core.

instruments.name: Weather, pressure and magnetic sensors
instruments.role: Recorded wind, air pressure, temperature and magnetic signals that affect the seismic data.

paragraphs: InSight left the most tightly instrumented patch of ground on another planet. The mission data records two inactive entries.

entities.name: InSight lander
entities.text: A three-legged lander with a robotic arm, cameras and solar panels. Dust gradually covered the panels and cut its power.

entities.name: SEIS seismometer
entities.location: Deployed on the surface near the lander
entities.text: A copper-coloured instrument placed on the ground by the arm, covered by a domed wind and thermal shield that kept winds and temperature swings from disturbing its sensors.

paragraphs: InSight ended because of power, not damage. Dust built up on its solar panels and the lander’s power generation steadily declined. Contact was last made on 15 December 2022. After two consecutive missed communication sessions NASA retired the mission and set 15 December 2022 as the end-of-mission date.

status.label: Instrument status
status.value: All instruments inactive; HP3 did not reach the planned depth

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: The lander and the seismometer under its dome, in Elysium Planitia

paragraphs: InSight looked deeper into Mars than any earlier mission and proved that the planet is still seismically active. It gave scientists the first comprehensive map of another planet’s deep interior.
Its method is as important as its results. Placing the seismometer on the ground, under a shield, and listening for years, showed that planetary seismology can work, even with a single station.

inherited.before: Before InSight, no one had measured Mars’s interior. Earlier landers carried seismometers mounted on the lander deck, where winds and vibrations from the spacecraft itself interfered with the signal. So the size of the Martian core, whether it is liquid and whether the planet is seismically active were all open questions.

instrument.name: SEIS (Seismic Experiment for Interior Structure)
instrument.how: SEIS was placed directly on the ground by the lander’s arm and then covered with a dome that shields it from wind and heat swings. A seismometer measures the motion of the ground by the lag of a suspended mass, and SEIS was designed for extremely quiet signals. A marsquake sends waves through the planet; they speed up, slow down, bend and reflect at the boundaries between layers. By timing them, scientists can work out what is inside.

evidence: SEIS detected more than 1,300 marsquakes and meteorite impacts over the mission.
Waves that travelled through the deep interior and reflected off the core boundary revealed a core that is completely liquid, slightly larger and less dense than predicted.
Radio tracking of the lander also measured how Mars wobbles as it spins, which depends on the core.
inherited.breakthrough: Mars has a crust, mantle and liquid core that can now be mapped, and the planet is still seismically active.

directVsInterpreted.text: More than 1,300 recorded marsquakes; travel times and shapes of seismic waves.
That the core is liquid, and its size and density, deduced from how waves cross it.
What the core is made of. A less dense core suggests lighter elements mixed in with iron, but the composition is not directly measured.

inherited.legacy: InSight data are now the reference for how a rocky planet other than Earth and the Moon is built inside. They are used to test models of how planets form and cool.
inherited.technology: InSight also proved technology: robotic placement of a seismometer on another planet, a wind and thermal shield that can protect it, and the use of a radio signal to measure a planet’s spin.

after: A liquid core, larger and less dense than predicted
More than 1,300 marsquakes recorded
The first map of the crust, mantle and core

spotlight.headline: The first map of another planet’s deep interior
spotlight.text: On 19 December 2018 InSight’s arm lifted a copper-coloured instrument and set it down on Martian ground. It was the first time a seismometer had been robotically placed on another planet. In the following years the little instrument heard enough quakes to map the layers of Mars from crust to core.
evidence: More than 1,300 marsquakes detected
Liquid core, slightly larger and less dense than predicted
Seismic activity shown to be ongoing

numbers.label: marsquakes detected
landed mass
length of the robotic arm that placed the instruments
planned mission length (about two Earth years); InSight worked about four
day the seismometer was placed on the ground

ripple.title: Planetary seismology
ripple.text: InSight showed the technique works on Mars, and the methods are being applied to future seismometers.

ripple.title: Models of planet formation
ripple.text: A liquid core that is less dense than predicted changes assumptions about what Mars is made of.

ripple.title: Instrument design
ripple.text: The shield and ground placement are now reference designs for quiet sensors on other worlds.

unanswered.question: How much heat flows out of Mars?
unanswered.text: The heat probe that was meant to measure it could not burrow to the planned depth, so Mars’s heat flow has not been measured directly. The composition of the liquid core is also open.
unanswered.future: A future seismic or heat-flow network on Mars could answer both.

notes: Confirmed: SEIS provided by CNES with PI at IPGP; dome shield; 19 Dec 2018 placement; 2.4 m arm; planned one Martian year; image captions; mission data for >1,300 marsquakes, liquid core, dust, end date, mass, coordinates.

From general knowledge, please verify: landing date November 2018; HP3 failing to burrow (NASA ended attempts in January 2021); RISE and APSS roles; earlier lander seismometers limited by deck mounting (supported by a 2019 news article); Cerberus-type details deliberately omitted.

dawn.tagline: The first spacecraft to orbit two worlds, and to visit a dwarf planet, now circling Ceres in silence.
dawn.dek: Using ion propulsion, Dawn orbited Vesta and then Ceres, revealing a dry, battered protoplanet and a dwarf planet with salty bright spots.

paragraphs: Vesta and Ceres are the two largest bodies in the main asteroid belt. They are relics from around 4.6 billion years ago, when planets were forming, and they turned out very different: one rocky and dry, the other icy and wet. The mission data states Dawn’s goals as determining the processes and conditions that produced and modified these protoplanets and understanding the role of water in the evolution of asteroids.

Dawn launched on 27 September 2007 with a launch mass of 1,218 kg. It was powered by solar-electric ion propulsion: a very gentle engine that expels ionised xenon gas and builds up speed slowly. That efficiency was what allowed one spacecraft to orbit one world, leave, and orbit another.
Dawn spent 14 months orbiting Vesta, then used its ion engines to leave and travel to Ceres. It was the first spacecraft to orbit two separate bodies beyond Earth.

timeline.title: Launch
timeline.text: Dawn leaves Earth.

timeline.title: Orbit around Vesta
timeline.text: Dawn begins a year of orbiting the giant asteroid.

timeline.title: Full view of Vesta
timeline.text: A rotation sequence from 5,200 km shows craters and grooves around the equator.

timeline.title: 14 months at Vesta
timeline.text: Dawn maps its surface, gravity and composition.

timeline.title: Arrival at Ceres
timeline.text: Dawn becomes the first spacecraft to orbit a dwarf planet.

timeline.title: Mapping Ceres
timeline.text: Dawn descends to lower orbits and resolves the bright spots in Occator Crater.

timeline.title: Last transmission
timeline.text: Dawn transmits for the last time after running out of hydrazine.

timeline.title: Mission concluded
timeline.text: NASA announces the end of the mission.

paragraphs: Three instruments did most of the work, supported by radio tracking of the spacecraft itself, which measured each world’s gravity.

instruments.name: Framing Camera
instruments.role: Took the images of Vesta and Ceres that revealed their craters, grooves, mountains and bright spots.

instruments.name: Visible and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIR)
instruments.role: Identified minerals, salts and organic compounds from the way surfaces reflect light.

instruments.name: Gamma Ray and Neutron Detector (GRaND)
instruments.role: Measured elements, including hydrogen, in the top metre of the surface.

instruments.name: Radio science (gravity)
instruments.role: Used tiny changes in the spacecraft’s speed to measure each world’s interior structure.

paragraphs: The mission data lists one object: the Dawn spacecraft, inactive, in orbit around Ceres. It did not land there.

entities.name: Dawn spacecraft
entities.text: A bus with two long solar arrays, three xenon ion thrusters and a set of small hydrazine thrusters for orientation. When the hydrazine ran out, Dawn could no longer point its antenna at Earth, and its mission ended.

paragraphs: Dawn did not crash. It ran out of the hydrazine fuel used to orient itself and point its antenna, which meant it could no longer talk to Earth. It transmitted for the last time on 31 October 2018, and NASA announced the end of the mission on 1 November 2018. It remains in a stable orbit around the dwarf planet Ceres, and is expected to stay there for decades.

status.label: Spacecraft status
status.value: Inactive, in a stable orbit around Ceres (it did not land)

paragraphs: Dawn was the first mission to visit a dwarf planet and the first to orbit two different bodies in the Solar System. It transformed the asteroid belt from a field of points of light into a place with geology, a story about water and, at Ceres, active salts.
It also proved that ion propulsion could power a flagship-class science mission.

inherited.before: Before Dawn, Vesta was suspected to be the source of a family of meteorites found on Earth, and the Hubble Space Telescope had seen a giant crater on it. Ceres was less known: Earth-based images showed a bright spot that nobody could explain, and nobody knew whether it had water.

instrument.name: Visible and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIR)
instrument.how: A spectrometer splits reflected sunlight into hundreds of colours, including infrared ones our eyes cannot see. Different minerals absorb different colours, so the pattern works like a fingerprint. VIR could map those fingerprints across Ceres. Combined with the camera, which showed what the spots looked like, it showed what the spots were made of.

evidence: Dawn’s camera found more than 300 bright spots, called faculae, sprinkled across Ceres. The brightest area sits in Occator Crater, which is 92 km across and 4 km deep, with a dome inside a smooth-walled pit.
The spectrometer identified the bright material as salts, principally sodium carbonate. This is what was left behind when briny water reached the surface and the water evaporated.
A 2017 study estimated the central bright area is about 4 million years old, while Occator Crater is about 34 million years old, so the activity came long after the impact.
In another crater, Ernutet, Dawn found evidence of organic material.
inherited.breakthrough: Ceres is not a frozen dead rock: it has been geologically active in the geologically recent past, and that activity involves salty water from below.

directVsInterpreted.text: Bright deposits, their salt composition, a dome in Occator and organic signatures at Ernutet.
That brines rose from below and left the salts, and that activity may be ongoing.
What the organics mean. They raise questions about chemistry that precedes life. They are not evidence of life.

inherited.legacy: Dawn’s Ceres results opened the idea that small, icy worlds may harbour brines, a theme now explored across the outer Solar System.
inherited.technology: Dawn proved the technology of ion propulsion for science missions: with it, one spacecraft visited and orbited two worlds, something chemical rockets could not do with the same mass.

before: A single unexplained bright spot on Ceres
Vesta suspected as the meteorite source
after: More than 300 bright salt deposits
Vesta confirmed as dry and differentiated, linked to meteorites
Evidence of brines and recent activity on Ceres

spotlight.headline: Ceres’ brightest spot is salt
spotlight.text: Hubble had shown Ceres with a bright spot and no explanation. Dawn resolved it into a cluster of intense deposits inside Occator Crater, with a dome at the centre. The deposits are salts, left when brine rose from below and its water evaporated. And they turned out to be much younger than the crater that holds them.
evidence: Occator Crater is 92 km across and 4 km deep
Sodium carbonate salts identified by the spectrometer
Central bright area about 4 million years old, crater about 34 million

numbers.source: NASA/JPL, “10 Things to Know About Dawn”

numbers.label: width and depth of Occator Crater
estimated ages in years of Cerealia Facula and Occator Crater

ripple.title: Ocean worlds thinking
ripple.text: Brine on a dwarf planet encouraged looking for brines on other small, icy worlds.

ripple.title: Meteorites on Earth
ripple.text: Dawn tied a family of Earth meteorites to a specific parent body, Vesta.

ripple.title: Electric propulsion
ripple.text: Electric propulsion has since been used on other deep-space missions.

unanswered.question: Is there still liquid under Ceres’ surface?
unanswered.text: Dawn showed that salty water reached the surface recently. It could not say whether a reservoir of brine still exists, how big it is, or where the organic material came from.
unanswered.future: Missions that would return to Ceres, possibly to bring back samples, have been proposed, but none is flying.

pioneer-10.tagline: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter, carrying a message in case anyone finds it.
pioneer-10.dek: Pioneer 10 proved the asteroid belt could be crossed, took the first close-up images of Jupiter and then headed out of the Solar System.

paragraphs: In February 1969 NASA approved a two-spacecraft project to explore Jupiter, managed by the Ames Research Center and built by TRW. Nobody knew whether a spacecraft could survive the asteroid belt, or Jupiter’s radiation, so the first goal was simply to find out.

Pioneer 10 launched on 2 March 1972, with a launch mass of 258 kg. It was spin-stabilised and was the first spacecraft to use all-nuclear electrical power. Its objectives in the mission data were to be the first to travel through the asteroid belt, and to obtain close-up images and data of Jupiter and its environment.

facts.label: Firsts
facts.value: Asteroid belt crossing; Jupiter close-ups; all-nuclear power

paragraphs: The journey to Jupiter took 640 days and about a billion kilometres. Along the way Pioneer 10 became the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt, then raced past Jupiter at about 126,000 km/h and was flung out of the inner Solar System.

timeline.title: Launch
timeline.text: Pioneer 10 leaves Earth.

timeline.title: Enters the asteroid belt
timeline.text: The first spacecraft to do so.

timeline.title: Emerges unscathed
timeline.text: Seven months later it leaves the belt without serious damage.

timeline.title: Jupiter imaging begins
timeline.text: Still about 16 million miles away, it starts imaging with its photopolarimeter.

timeline.title: Closest approach
timeline.text: At 02:26 UT it passes about 130,000 km from Jupiter. About 78 minutes later it passes behind the planet for a radio experiment.

timeline.title: Crosses Saturn’s orbit
timeline.text: Still outbound.

timeline.title: Routine contact ends
timeline.text: Because of budget limits, regular tracking stops when the spacecraft is 67 AU from Earth.

timeline.title: Overtaken by Voyager 1
timeline.text: Until then Pioneer 10 was the most distant human-made object.

timeline.title: Signal received
timeline.text: A ground team receives a signal that the spacecraft systems are nominal.

timeline.title: Last contact
timeline.text: The final faint telemetry is received.

paragraphs: Pioneer 10 carried a modest set of instruments, picked for a mission that was mostly a risk check on Jupiter’s environment.

instruments.name: Imaging Photopolarimeter
instruments.role: Built images of Jupiter and its moons strip by strip using the spacecraft’s spin; also measured polarised light.

instruments.name: Helium Vector Magnetometer
instruments.role: Measured the strength and direction of magnetic fields.

instruments.name: Infrared Radiometer
instruments.role: Measured temperatures in Jupiter’s atmosphere.

instruments.name: Quadrispherical Plasma Analyzer
instruments.role: Measured the solar wind and plasma near Jupiter.

instruments.name: Ultraviolet Photometer
instruments.role: Measured hydrogen and helium.

instruments.name: Charged Particle Instrument and Cosmic Ray Telescope
instruments.role: Charted radiation belts and energetic particles.

instruments.name: Meteoroid and asteroid/meteoroid detectors
instruments.role: Counted dust and particles encountered in the asteroid belt.

paragraphs: The mission data lists two items, both on the same machine: the spacecraft itself and its plaque.

entities.name: Pioneer 10 spacecraft
entities.location: Outbound on an escape trajectory toward interstellar space
entities.text: A spin-stabilised spacecraft with a large dish antenna facing Earth and radioisotope generators on booms. Its power fell below what its transmitter needed, and it went silent.

entities.name: Pioneer plaque
entities.location: Mounted to the spacecraft’s antenna support struts
entities.condition: Intact (as recorded in the mission data)
entities.text: A 6 by 9 inch gold-anodised aluminium plaque designed by Carl Sagan, Frank Drake and Linda Salzman Sagan. It shows a man and a woman, the Solar System, and the position of the Sun relative to 14 pulsars.

paragraphs: Pioneer 10 has three end dates and they are not the same. Routine contact ended on 31 March 1997 for budget reasons. A signal on 5 August 2000 showed the spacecraft was still working. The last faint telemetry arrived on 23 January 2003, and the mission data uses that date as the end. After that, its radioisotope power source had decayed below the level needed to power the transmitter.

Pioneer 10 is on an outward escape trajectory. It is not being tracked, so its present position can be calculated but not confirmed, and this archive makes no claim about whether it has crossed the heliopause. NASA has said it is heading generally toward the star Aldebaran, a journey of more than two million years.

status.label: Spacecraft status
status.value: Inactive, travelling outward on an escape trajectory

status.label: What physically remains
status.value: The whole spacecraft and its plaque, in motion

paragraphs: Pioneer 10 was the pathfinder. It showed that the asteroid belt could be crossed, that Jupiter’s radiation could be survived and measured, and that a spacecraft could be put on a path out of the Solar System. It was the first to do each of these.
Its plaque also began a tradition. The Golden Record on the Voyager spacecraft followed a few years later.

inherited.before: Before Pioneer 10, engineers did not know whether the asteroid belt would be a minefield of dust and rock, or what Jupiter’s radiation belts would do to a spacecraft. Jupiter’s magnetic field was known only from radio signals picked up on Earth. There were no close-up images of the planet.

instrument.name: Imaging Photopolarimeter
instrument.how: Pioneer 10 had no conventional camera. Its photopolarimeter looked out through a small telescope as the whole spacecraft spun. Each turn of the spacecraft swept one thin line across Jupiter, and as the spacecraft moved, the lines stacked up into an image. It also split the light by polarisation. Near Jupiter, though, the intense radiation damaged it.

evidence: More than 500 images of Jupiter and its moons came back, the first close-up pictures of the planet, along with photos of Callisto, Ganymede and Europa.
The charged-particle and magnetic instruments charted Jupiter’s radiation belts and located its magnetic field, which was massive, rotating with the planet and extending much farther than expected.
The meteoroid detectors measured how many particles the spacecraft met in the asteroid belt, and the spacecraft came out undamaged on 15 February 1973.
A photo of Io was taken but lost: the radiation near Jupiter overwhelmed the photopolarimeter.
inherited.breakthrough: The asteroid belt could be crossed safely and Jupiter’s radiation could be survived, which opened the door to later missions to the outer planets.

directVsInterpreted.text: Images, radiation levels, magnetic field measurements and particle counts.
That Jupiter is mostly liquid, and what the size of its magnetic field means about its interior.
That the asteroid belt is safe in general. It was safe along the one path Pioneer 10 took.

inherited.legacy: The radiation measurements and the successful belt crossing informed the design and trajectories of Voyager and later Jupiter missions.
inherited.technology: Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to use all-nuclear electrical power, and proved that a spin-stabilised design could return data from beyond 60 AU. Later, its tracking data helped scientists chase down an unexplained tiny acceleration, which has since been attributed to heat radiated from the spacecraft itself.

after: Belt crossed unscathed
Radiation belts charted
More than 500 images and a mapped magnetic field

spotlight.headline: A camera that lost Io to radiation
spotlight.text: Pioneer 10 flew closer to Jupiter than anything had before, and the planet fought back. The photopolarimeter took a picture of the volcanic moon Io, but the radiation was so intense that the image was lost. It is a negative result, but a valuable one: it told engineers how much shielding the next spacecraft would need.
evidence: Io image taken but lost to radiation
Closest approach about 130,000 km from the cloud tops
More than 500 images of Jupiter and its moons still returned

ripple.title: Voyager
ripple.text: Pioneer’s results guided Voyager’s design and routes, and its plaque inspired the Golden Record.

ripple.title: Pioneer 11
ripple.text: The sister spacecraft used Jupiter’s gravity to reach Saturn.

ripple.title: The Pioneer anomaly
ripple.text: A small unexplained acceleration in the tracking data was eventually explained by the spacecraft’s own heat.

unanswered.question: What is out there in the direction Pioneer 10 travelled?
unanswered.text: Pioneer 10 has been silent since 2003, so no instrument is reporting from the path it took. Its exact position can only be calculated, and the question of how the Sun’s environment varies from one direction to another remains open.
unanswered.future: Only the Voyager spacecraft are reporting from interstellar space, and each covers a single path.
